**Let Your Customers, Not a Formula, Decide How Much Parking You Need**

If you own a shop, parking is not an abstraction. You've watched a customer circle the block twice and then leave. So I understand why "eliminate parking minimums" sounds like a plan to hurt you. It isn't, and here is why.

A parking minimum is a rule requiring a set number of spaces per square foot or per seat, whether or not your business needs them. Removing it doesn't ban parking. It returns the decision to the person who knows the trade: you.

**Objection one: "Without mandates, no one will build parking, and customers will stop coming."** Developers who expect drivers to be their customers have every reason to provide spaces, and many still do in cities that scrapped minimums, including Buffalo, which did so in 2017. What changes is that a bakery doesn't need the same lot as a furniture warehouse. A structured space can cost $30,000 or more to build, and that cost lands in your rent or kills the project. Plenty of would-be owners never open because the old building can't fit the required stalls.

**Objection two: "New neighbors will under-provide, and their customers will crowd my curb."** That is a real risk, but the minimum is a clumsy defense. The better tool is managing the curb itself: time limits, modest meter pricing, and, most importantly, spending the meter revenue on the district's own sidewalks and lighting. Priced curb space turns over, which means more customers per space. A free space that's occupied all day by one commuter's car is worth nothing to your register.

Minimums were written from traffic manuals calibrated to suburban peak days, then applied to Main Street. Ask your council to replace the formula with flexibility and a plan for the curb. Your next competitor may be less constrained, but so will your next tenant, your next expansion, and your next neighbor.
